text_fidelity_a:
Everlast Folding Exercise Mat I had a hip replacement over a year ago, and things haven't gone as planned. I'm still in physical therapy. It's been discouraging, to say the least. I'm only 50, and people 20 years older than me recover better. I've been losing motivation to do my exercises at home, because I get on a damn yoga mat, and everything hurts. I got online to find an exercise mat I'd like more, trying to reinvigorate my motivation. I thought this would be "ok" . Somehow I thought the 2" of thickness would probably be a lot of air along with cushioning. I was wrong: This mat is great. If you're in PT a lot, like I have been, you will appreciate and LOVE THIS MAT.

Other than the excellent cushioning (I weigh 180 lbs, at 5'8), I love that I don't have to roll it. The handles are perfectly positioning to pick it up straight, fold it, and tuck it behind a door. The fold doesn't create a big gap at all when it's flat, you really can't even notice it. The thing doesn't slide easily. It doesn't have grippy material, but for some reason, it barely moved on my hardwood floor, which is great when you're doing PT exercises. A slippy mat would have been dangerous. I can't even think of one thing wrong with it. If you are doing PT, or know someone who is, get this mat. Would be a great gift for someone doing PT.
text_fidelity_b: Everlast Folding Exercise Mat

text_fidelity_a:
Nordic Walking Poles for Individuals 6’ 2” – 6’ 3” = 132.5cm SWIX of Norway. All 32 Lengths Coming Soon 1-Piece Non-Collapsible. #1 for Hiking, Trekking, Physical Therapy. My review is primarily geared towards people who are interested in learning the Nordic walking techniques and are looking for inexpensive, appropriate walking sticks. It is also a comparison of the sticks offered here and the so-called “crappy Chinese” anti-shock, telescoping sticks. I have purchased both and am including photos below.

I started Nordic walking about 3 or 4 years ago. At the time, I wasn’t sure that this was something I would continue to do and did not want to spend a small fortune on equipment that would, once again, end up unused in a closet. But I was having trouble walking even a short distance (100 ft. or so) without excruciating burning in my legs and back, so thought I needed to give this a shot. I sprang for the cheap sticks and boy, am I glad I did! Within a few weeks, I was walking a mile with very little discomfort. That distance might be laughable to some, but to me, it was a miracle!

But honestly, it had less to do with the type of sticks than it did with learning the proper technique. There are many videos available that demonstrate the technique and anyone interested should spend some time watching them. It is not difficult to learn. In fact once you get the rhythm it’s like riding a bike…you don’t forget how to do it.

As far as the poles go, I see little difference in them. Perhaps at a higher price difference there is, but it’s still more about learning the skills.

Cheap Chinese poles (the black ones in the photos): When I bought mine I made some modifications. The rubber tips that were included wore out quickly. I replaced those with the boot type of tip which has lasted all these years and many miles. The tips are deeply grooved like snow tires and they do pick up small pieces of sand. This will make them slip some on asphalt, but it’s fairly easy to flick a grain of sand out and continue your walk. I also replaced the sponge rubber grip just below the handle (because it tore easily) with some closed cell tubing that I found online. That wasn’t entirely necessary because you never or rarely grab the poles in that area. I should have just eliminated it altogether.

These poles are the twist lock telescoping type (not the clamp type), which is handy when you don’t know what length pole you need in the beginning. But once adjusted, it is a PITA to collapse or readjust them. They do have a scale on them that shows the length you’ve set them to, so if you get these, make a note or find some way of marking the length. I never collapse mine anymore, because I want to start walking immediately, not fiddle with adjustments. However, if you need to pack your walking sticks, and don’t mind messing with the twist locks, this is certainly a consideration when you buy. I have never had the twist locks fail or accidently collapse once snuggly hand tightened.

These poles also have the anti-shock springs. It makes them heavier and, yes, they make a rattling noise every time the pole hits the pavement. Their extra weight does makes their footfall more forceful. I see no advantage to the springs at this point, but I’ve heard that they are helpful when going down steep terrain. Can’t say, because most of my walking is on fairly level pavement. BUT, DO NOT let the noise stop you from buying if you don’t want to spend a lot of money in the beginning. Getting you walking again is far more important than any minor rattles.

The handle grips are very comfortable and include a strap for your hands to go up through. I found these straps were much more comfortable for me and more convenient to use. Just remember to insert your hand up from the bottom of the strap.

Overall, these poles have a bigger diameter than the “real” ones and are slightly heavier. However, I think the few added ounces actually give you a better upper body and arm workout than the lighter poles. So, to me, the extra weight could be advantageous. Cost for these poles was 14.95 for each pole (@29.90). The Leki replacement tips cost $17.31 with tax, and I highly recommend them. I’m not including the rubber grip which is not necessary, so my actual cost was $47.21 with tax.

Real Nordic walking sticks (blue in the photos): As noted above, these are somewhat lighter, thinner, nonadjustable, non-spring-loaded poles. It is important that you order the right length. They adjustable have glove like straps attached to the handle.

Personally, I’m not entirely pleased with these particular straps. As you will see in the photos, their design leaves something to be desired. I have circled the points where they irritate my hands. And here, I will have to make some kind of modification if I want to use these poles for an extended time. The gloves interfere with wearing my fitness watch and the binding on some corners should be more rounded instead of squared off. Strapping your hand in or out, by means of Velcro strips, is awkward; and should you need to let go of your poles if you fall, you’re out of luck. There is a means of length adjustment (by pulling upward on the handle top) which is lacking in the Chinese poles, but it doesn’t solve the rubbing issues, since the part which cradles your hand doesn’t change position. After I have used these poles more, I may try to fashion a strap comparable to the ones on the Chinese poles.

The handles themselves are thinner and (though you shouldn’t be clasping them tightly) may be more suited to smaller hands. I can’t say for sure, but they are still comfortable.

I have a gut feeling that the boot tips on these sticks will wear quickly, needing to be replaced often. However, they do not have the deep tread of the Leki replacement tips and do not pick up grains of rock or sand, so that is an advantage as far as sliding on pavement goes. I will most likely replace these stock tips with the Leki ones and just deal with the rocks.

The cost for these poles (before any changes I may make) is, at this writing, $77.45 including tax and/or shipping. I am, otherwise, perfectly satisfied with these “real” Nordic walking sticks. They are light, not noisy and do what they’re supposed to do.

Both poles need some slight modification, but their functions are identical. Once again, it’s about technique, not one type of pole compared to another. Please do not let any hype make your decision. It’s far more important that you get out there and start walking.
I'm awarding 5 stars to either kind of pole. Both work pretty much equally.
text_fidelity_b: Nordic Walking Poles for Individuals 6’ 2” – 6’ 3” = 132.5cm SWIX of Norway. All 32 Lengths Coming Soon 1-Piece Non-Collapsible. #1 for Hiking, Trekking, Physical Therapy.

For the amount and type of running that I do, the AiRunTech hydration running belt is perfect, and I suspect it also works great for the really long-distance runners.

Some features I found really useful:
- The combination of velcro adjustment plus a partially elastic band allowed me to fit the running belt exactly how I wanted it. After it's set, a buckle let's me get the belt on and off very quickly.
- The 10-oz water bottles fit securely in the belt and on my hips. The curved shape of the bottles align with the body contour better than straight bottles. An extra elastic loop makes sure each bottle stays in place and doesn't bounce.
- The main pocket fits my iphone 13 pro max securely.
- Lightweight

Additional features I didn't use:
- Earphone outlet (I use bluetooth earphones)
- Energy gel loops (the distances I run are not long enough to need energy gel)

The photos on the Amazon description page show the runners wearing the belt with the pockets and water bottles on the front part of their bodies. I didn't find the belt to be comfortable in that position--my legs hit the bottles when running. Instead, I've worn it with the pocket and bottles on my back, and then I barely notice I am wearing the belt with its bottles.

By the way, the belt works for long hikes too!

After the experience with the AiRunTech hydration running belt, I got another one for my wife that should arrive soon. This one has the smaller 6-oz. bottles.

text_fidelity_a: Brunton 7DNL Baseplate Map Compass I've trekked many miles, guided by the same Brunton 7DNL baseplate compass I received from my wilderness survival camp counselor, decades ago. While it's not as rugged as some other models, for the price you can buy 2 or 3 of them so you have spares.  As well, you won't feel as guilty should one disappear, or be damaged.  Its compact size makes it handy, but also makes it a little harder to get precise bearings.  It also doesn't have true declination adjustment, only an etched-in scale, which can lead to some issues if you forget this nuance.  For casual trips, I'm quite comfortable with relying on the Brunton 7DNL.  For anything more critical, it's my backup compass (to a more-expensive [[ASIN:B000FEWA6S Suunto M-3DL Compass]], which I tend to baby).

text_fidelity_a:
FINIS Swimp3 1GB Waterproof MP3 Player I bought this primarily to listen to Podcasts and some music while swimming laps. When it arrived, I was pleased with the hardware quality and ease of use. I loaded up some music and Podcasts and headed for the pool. It was relatively easy to clip the units to my goggles. The controls could be better, but are not terrible. I put it on, started playing a Podcast, put in my earplugs and started swimming. I had been concerned that my goggles might leak or come off during turns with these units clipped on, but it was not a problem at all.
The problem, though, was the sound. If sitting perfectly still underwater, it sounds decent. Pretty much on par with my 30-year-old one-speaker clock radio. However, even with earplugs, the noise of swimming and rushing water overpowers it. If I play familiar songs I can tell what I am listening to and somewhat enjoy them. However, forget about the spoken word. I had to turn the volume up really loud to be able to make out most of what was said on the Podcast due to distortion and background noise. And then it was just too loud to be enjoyable. In fact, I am sure that others in the pool could hear some sound from it. I tried to adjust it in every possible way, and followed the instructions precisely.
This seems like a good idea, but I am disappointed, especially for the cost.

Pros: Solid design, no earphones or earbuds, can still wear earplugs, easy to wear, stays on goggles and doesn't pull them off, easy to load songs.
Cons: Price, 1 GB of storage is a total insult, limited features and controls for an MP3 player, poor sound quality overshadows all else.
text_fidelity_b: FINIS Swimp3 1GB Waterproof MP3 Player

text_fidelity_a:
Kershaw Junk Yard Dog 2.2 Composite Blade Knife I have no need for the fighting knives, or pseudo-fighting knives, that predominate that seem to predominate in all the catalogs and websites. I was trained as a Marine, years ago, and so have enough knowledge of hand to hand combat to realize that to effectively fight with a knife requires years of training and practice. Besides, a folding knife for such purposes is nonsense.
What I required was a practical, everyday utility knife for town and country, the mall and the hunters camp. At first glance, I thought this knife a bit large for that purpose but it is actually perfect. The blade is a perfect combination of very hard but brittle steel, with superior edge holding abilities, for the edge and much tougher, flexible steel for the "backbone" supporting it. Of course, the Japanese have been doing this for centuries in their Samurai swords. Blade wide and thick enough for good practical function without excess that only adds to weight and provides little practical value. The grip fits the human hand ideally. It fits my hand (size 7.5-8 glove) perfectly. The thumb and forefinger "pinch" close together in their respective, appropriately shaped, knurled "notches" giving one a superior grip for slicing, skinning, stabbing motions and provide a barrier to the hand slipping forward into the blade. The rest of the grip, is nicely shaped to enhance your hold again without excess. The scales are G10 epoxy - amazingly tough and strong but light - with a perfect degree of abrasive crosshatching. One can easily open AND CLOSE it with one hand, something one might need to do when aloft striking the topsail in a squall and wondering what possessed you do do such a thing without a riggers knife on your belt. Yes, it's made in the USA but who cares; like my fine shotguns and tools, with some things, the world is one community.
text_fidelity_b: Kershaw Junk Yard Dog 2.2 Composite Blade Knife

Garmin fēnix 5, Premium and Rugged Multisport GPS Smartwatch, Granite Blue Functionally speaking, this watch is pretty full featured. It has basic mapping and will accomodate most common activities very well. I like the build quality as well. I don't use any of the health monitoring features, so those are disabled to save battery life. Battery life is OK overall, not great. It loses about 8-10% on a one hour hike.

The reason for the one star review has to do with the non-replaceable battery, and the fact that this is a $500+ watch. I am on year two of owning this watch now and have seen about a 30% drop in battery life. That's pretty bad if you ask me. I predict I'll get another couple years out of it before the battery becomes unreliable for anything more than a run around the neighborhood. As such I can't recommend this watch at all as I think it is a very poor value... 3-5 years of use for a watch that costs upwards of $1000 for the high end models is totally unacceptable.

I've got an old Forerunner 101 that I bought back in the early 2000s that I prefer over the Fenix. It's comically bulky, but runs on AAA batteries, so you can just keep going and going and going. I wish Garmin would have kept the Forerunner line.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin fēnix 5, Premium and Rugged Multisport GPS Smartwatch, Granite Blue

text_fidelity_a: CamelBak Men's Palisade Hike Hydration Pack - Integrated Rain Cover Finally got a chance to take the bag out and put it though it’s paces. We don’t have any camping trips planned for now, but we put a towel and 10 lbs of weight and off we went. He’s 6 feet and skinny for reference. Took it for a thirty minute walk in 90 degrees F and 49% humidity. The pack felt good. The air gap was great, and kept him from overheating. He said the bag sat well and didn’t shift once secured. He is right handed and a lot like my other hiking backpacks, there is only a zipper pocket in the left waist band. This is because you don’t usually reach across to get something in your waist pocket on a hike. The right side is a non zip folded pocket. The rain cover stuffs in a Velcro pocket on the bottom and fits snugly over the entire pack. The large roomy main compartment fits everything I would need for a weekend hike, or a long day hike. Food, camp stove, change of clothing, single man tent, jacket and the large capacity reservoir. There is a hook to put the reservoir on so it doesn’t slip down as you empty the bladder. The bite valve is the standard camelback with shut off (this is important if you have ever been hiking and broken your bite valve and didn’t have time to dig out a spare until base camp.) this is Not a carry your laptop and tootle around town pack. This is a well made solid day/weekend hiker. Yes it would be nice to have a small inner zip pocket, but that’s what carabiners and dry sacks are for. It has a mesh two compartment pocket, and a larger pocket the whole bag length. Water reservoir has its own zippered compartment, and there is one center small zip pocket for quick access item like headlamp. Has a large adjustable mesh pocket on the outside that you can put a helmet, or ground roll. Can’t wait for camping to open up again, I may just steal this from my husband for scout campouts. Product free in exchange for an honest review.
text_fidelity_b: CamelBak Men's Palisade Hike Hydration Pack - Integrated Rain Cover

Sunny Health & Fitness Premium Treadmill Features Auto Incline, Dedicated Speed Buttons, Bluetooth Connectivity, Built-In Speakers, Digital Performance Display and Pulse Sensors - SF-T7515 This is a solid purchase for the price. It is relatively easy to assemble (some of the pieces didn't line up correctly and required some manhandling to make it work), it is easy to use, and it feels solid. The thing I truly love is the auto incline adjustment. I can't imagine having to do that manually.

Main issue is the sound system. Terrible to say the least. Speakers buzz unless you adjust cord just right (and then the vibration from running will get it out of whack again). The sound controls on the treadmill do not work, and the sound is generally bad. For me, not a deal-breaker. Just disappointing. Also, there is an occasional squeaking in the treadmill that is irritating but, again, not a problem so far. One thing to be aware of, though. The track is narrow. It is fine for me and my daughter, but my husband hits the sides pretty regularly.

Like I said, fine for the price. But all three of agree that next purchase will be a big upgrade. We wanted to test the treadmill-use waters, and this was a great first purchase.

text_fidelity_a:
Total Gym XLS Men/Women Universal Total Body Training Home Gym Workout Machine with Squat Stand, Leg Pull, 2 Ankle Cuffs, and Exercise Chart I just wanted to clear this up, this is the same exact package that is sold by Total Gym Direct! The only difference is that TG Direct offers the AbCrunch as a bonus, but their package is more expensive and you can purchase the Abcrunch on Amazon and still be way below the cost of purchasing the package from TG! I ordered the Abcrunch, which comes with a DVD, and the Weight Bar and still paid way below the 60% off price of TG Direct. I would say to wait until you get your TG before purchasing any attachments because I received a promo code with my TG for $20 and $30 off for accessories to use on the TotalGymCatalog dot com. This Total Gym came with 5 DVDs (workouts at every level and includes a pilates dvd), the Pilates package, wall chart, training deck and holder, wing attachment. Everything you need to workout!

There is no assembly, it comes fully assembled. I do recommend watching the set up dvd so you do not hurt yourself setting this up and you fully understand how it folds and unfolds. I did my first workout yesterday and I really feel it today. This machine is as smooth as butter! It is very quiet and appears to be of good solid quality. I bought a lesser quality type machine similar to this years ago and the difference is like night and day. My boyfriend is 6'4 and has no problems working out on this machine. The bench is almost 47" long x 16" wide and most of the exercises are done with your legs either bent up and crossed or sitting on your legs or with them hanging to the sides of the bench. This machine is 90" long and even doing squats there is still plenty of room.

The workouts are fun to do and don't take that much time. I was shocked how fast time went by as I was working out. That is what keeps people motivated. The workout never felt redundant. I feel fortunate to have a room dedicated to working out because it is not a small machine and I will leave it unfolded. In a small apartment this might feel like an elephant sitting in the room, but if you are willing to fold it up after each workout, it folds up very compactly.
Another bonus, if you have amazon prime you receive this machine in 2 days of ordering it!!! Whereas, the TG Direct site may take 10days! I am very happy with my purchase and will update if I notice any changes with this machine.
If you are looking for a less expensive Total Gym you might want to check out the Total Gym 1800 Club package. It is 399. and comes with many of the same equipment as this package. I just happen to come across it on youtube. In fact, watching the video, it looked as if it came with the AbCrunch. It is worth checking out if this package is not in your budget. Now that I have the XLS, I do not see much of a difference between the two machines except for the price and change in the bench style. There may be other differences, but it looks to be very similar and at a much lower price!
Update 7/27/2012 - I have been using the TG every other day with the beginning DVD and LOVING it!! I get really excited about working out now. Using the DVD is truly like having a personal trainer and I really sweat with the workout. I am so happy that I made this purchase and would recommend to anyone at any level wanting to get in shape. It gives a great cardio and toning/strengthening workout! At first I was a little worried I wasn't going to be able to keep up, but I just kept doing the best I could and now I love it and can't wait to work out. On days that I am not on the TG, I work out on my recumbent bike and am amazed how I feel now just in this short time. Sometimes I use the TG and the Bike on the same day and am working on doing that more.
text_fidelity_b: Total Gym XLS Men/Women Universal Total Body Training Home Gym Workout Machine with Squat Stand, Leg Pull, 2 Ankle Cuffs, and Exercise Chart

4 cubes butter, softened
2 heaping cups dark brown sugar (packed, then heap that shiz)
½ cups white sugar
2 tablespoons vanilla
1 ½ teaspoon salt
1 ½ teaspoons baking soda
3 eggs
6 cups flour
1 bag chocolate chips (semi-sweet or sweet)

Flash Personal Cooking System An absolutely awesome cooking system. Fast, fast, fast! Our initial use for the system will be to boil water for single serve instant coffee packets and to re-hydrate freeze dried food which will keep us and perhaps others happy while camping with the scouts.

Here's a common sense but helpful hint for someone using the Jetboil system for the first time - a no-brainer for anyone who has already cooked with this system:

- If you're just boiling water to pour into another vessel or coffee cup for example, go ahead and fully snap the lid on before beginning your boil. You can conveniently pour through the sipping hole.
- If you're boiling water for the purpose of adding food to the pot such as ramen for example, either lay the lid loosely on top or leave it off altogether.

Why? Because once you snap the lid all the way on and the contents come to a boil you'll burn your fingers trying to get it off unless you use a hot pad or other insulating material.

Highly recommended.

Wurkkos DL30 Scuba Diving Flashlight - Scuba Dive Light Super Bright Max 3600 Lumen with 5000K 90CRI,100m Underwater Flashlight IPX-8 Waterproof Submersible Flashlight with USB Charger This flashlight is a bit heavier than others in this size range. I think that is leaning more toward the battery size. The 21700 battery weighs 2.5 ounces whereas the 18650 is 1.5 ounces. The flashlight without the 21700 battery weighs 4.9 ounces. Another thing is it gets very warm from holding it in your hand on high mode for 5 minutes. A few minutes longer and it gets HOT and almost hard to hold unless you are wearing gloves. With this said the flashlight is designed for diving and stays a lot cooler under water. I submerged it in cool water and the flashlight does not get more than warm on high mode. It is the 3 LEDs that cause all the heat.

I love the brightness and the ease of turning the switch on and off. The 3 brightness settings are a good feature in my opinion and work flawlessly. To show how bright the high setting is, I included a picture of our stove with kitchen light off and standing about 7 feet back and no camera flash. If you store the flashlight for long periods of time, or if traveling and want to make sure the flashlight doesn't accidently turn on, you can just turn the tail cap backwards less than 1 turn and the flashlight is totally off. It works, I tested it! Wonderful!! The lens is very solid and thick. It appears to be nearly indestructible. Another feature is this item comes with a cover adapter for using the smaller 18650 battery that is standard in most flashlights. The 18650 wouldn't have as long a running time but runs a little cooler using this flashlight above water. We tested a fully charged 18650 on high for 5 minutes and it drained the battery to 64 percent. It is also just a bit less bright but noticeable. Testing the 21700 battery fully charged for 5 minutes above water drained the battery to 87 percent and when putting it back to charge it finished to 100 percent in about 17 minutes. We used a MiBoxer 8 battery charger that shows percentages while charging. Amazon sells them and we love it.

This flashlight in my opinion really is best underwater use. I also think if it was used as a normal flashlight and running it for 15 minutes or more on high on a hot evening could burn out the LEDs from the heat. The manual does not mention this and it says the flashlight has a built in ATR (advanced temperature regulation) and will reduce the power under certain situations of excessive heat to prevent overheating.

If you just wanted to use it above water for shorter times to find something lost like your wife's wedding ring because she got mad at you, this little gem is excellent and fits into most any size pocket. But it is SO bright you really do NOT want to look into it, and also have to be careful not to shine it in anyone’s face, and that includes pets.

Overall this is a great flashlight and I recommend it for quality and value!
text_fidelity_b: Wurkkos DL30 Scuba Diving Flashlight - Scuba Dive Light Super Bright Max 3600 Lumen with 5000K 90CRI,100m Underwater Flashlight IPX-8 Waterproof Submersible Flashlight with USB Charger

Great for beginners or someone just needing a cheaper option.
12/29/11 UPDATE_ Got to try these out for the first time (not real deep snow- but enough to give them a trial run) These shoes are really nice. I tromped around for about 30 mins and had very few problems (main problem was some ice build up on my heel as I crossed a wet area and the water froze on my boot heel- not a big deal as it can happen with any snowshoe). The bindings did hold well and did not loosen at all. One shoe did seem to be toeing in a bit but that was probably an adjustment issue (it was also a new pair of boots I was trying out.) I'm gonna hopefully get out in some deeper snow next week (yea Lake Effect!)
1/15/12 UPDATE2- Finally got some REAL snow (18+ inches!) and tried these out at my hilly property in the deep woods. AMAZING how well they worked. It was pretty cold (hovering around 16° F in the sun) and the woods were untouched by anything but a few deer and turkeys. These shoes performed great. They never slipped and I did not have to adjust the bindings at all. They do seem to make a bit of noise as far as the bindings creaking (at these temps not to surprising), but nothing broke or loosened. Walked for a little over an hour; over logs, thru brush, uphill, downhill, level, tight twisty area, open fields, deep drifts, and even a snowmobile trail (that crosses the front of our property). These preformed as good as any other shoe. A bonus is I found I really liked the poles- so much so that I gave one to my wife and she really liked using it too. All in all a great purchase- These honestly hover on a 5 star rating- I did have to take away for the pole bag not being attached some way- also the poles are nearly impossible to closeup once they get cold (I think a bit of frost gets into the loosening cam and freezes the pole in place as once they warmed up there were no problems) also there is no place to store the rubber protection cap from the pole. The one show still seemed to toe in a bit- but I only notice it in very shallow snow (less than 6 inches) and the toe binding still only rachets to a certain point and then slips (still not an issue as it is snug enough). Oh and of course the noise factor (not real bad but your not gonna sneak up on anything with these on)
text_fidelity_b: Snowshoes for Adult Unisex,Fully Adjustable Bindings, Lightweight Material, Hard Pack Grip Teeth,Outdoor Aluminum Alloy Material

Sunlite Cloud-9 Bicycle Suspension Cruiser Saddle, Cruiser Gel, Tri-color Black If you have the type of seat post where the saddle rails are sandwiched/clamped between two contoured plates this saddle might not work on your seat post clamp. This saddle comes with one of those rotary, rotating, claw-type clamps and the saddle likely works fine with that included clamp. However better bike seat posts can't use the included claw clamp type -- they must use their own sandwich-type. Technically, this saddle still should still mount but the distance between the rails was too wide. If you are confused about the difference do a web search for 'bike seat rail clamp' and you'll see the two different families of clamps.

I would have thought that the measured distance between saddle rails would be standardized but the rails on this saddle were just a very few millimeters too wide for both my sandwich-type clamps (it failed to mount on the two different seat post clamps I tried it on). The distance could maybe be lessened by clamping the rails, in a vice, for example, or using some other tool but I decided to return it rather than mess with it..

Otherwise it seemed okay, maybe quite a bit on the stiff side for a gel saddle.
text_fidelity_b: Sunlite Cloud-9 Bicycle Suspension Cruiser Saddle, Cruiser Gel, Tri-color Black

text_fidelity_a:
Swingbyte 2 Golf Training Device - Golf’s Most Trusted Mobile Swing Analyzer - Includes Mobile App for iPhone and Android The app that accompanies this and the way it works is simple and very neat. I have yet to have a chance to check it vs more expensive industry standards like GC2 or trackman BUT for the most part these devices are accurate unto themselves and it's user error that throws them off.

It does NOT do carry distance (which makes sense if you think about it, it doesn't see what the ball is doing). If you duff a shot fat and hit the deck before the ball, it will register that as your strike.

It has a very cool animation and 3D manipulated graphic and pretty much all the important info in terms of face angle/path/AoA/speed/shaft lean. All very good for the home golf nerd that doesn't have regular access to the big machines.

Where it falls short and loses a star from my perspective is this: The mounting system needs a good bit of work. I left it in my car on a hot day inside the little carrying case it comes in (it latches to a little plastic dowel) and when doing so I THINK it melted the rubber grippers that grab onto the club shaft. So now it doesn't have enough tension to hold onto smooth steel shafts (like on irons). So after a few solid strikes taking divots or some poorly struck shots that rattle the club you will notice that the device is no longer in line with your club face. Who knows how long it's been that way so unless you check every time your data for the day could be total garbage. Another thing, the cover that protects the USB charging port is ALSO the aligning mark. This presents two problems. 1 the darn thing keeps opening and flopping around while I try to swing. 2 This alignment mark which is suppose to assist in the ultimate accuracy of the device is on a component that is NOT securely fashioned onto the device itself.

Bottom line: Quite a fun and when used carefully possibly quite accurate tool to help you make your swing easier to quantify and tangible. Not perfect but maybe there will be a Swingbyte 3 that will address these things :)
text_fidelity_b: Swingbyte 2 Golf Training Device - Golf’s Most Trusted Mobile Swing Analyzer - Includes Mobile App for iPhone and Android

This extra illumination of this light has made a significant difference for me when commuting at night. I used to avoid areas with low illumination. The XOSS illuminates the ground in front like a car headlight allowing me to ride in total darkness. I tilt the light so can see everything coming at me from about 20-30 feet away, which is enough time to react at my normal riding speed.

I have also used both the automatic on/off motion sensor and standard on/off modes and they each worked well.

The handlebar attachment/removal system allows me to use the XOSS as a flashlight (have done this several times) and more easily charge it. However, the attachment clip has an issue - if you tighten it onto the handlebars too much, the screw will enter a hole on the bottom of the light and restrict it from being put on or removed. Be aware...

Recommended!

(update) The bracket snapped under fairly normal usage. Maybe it was the cold weather making the plastic a bit brittle... Rather than toss the light or turn it into a flashlight, I 3D printed a replacement part. You can find it on thingiverse. Just search for "XOSS Enfitnix Bike Headlight Bracket"

text_fidelity_a:
Simmons 20-60X60 Venture Black Fmcwptripodhard/Soft Case This old bird still has some of the original low power hunting scopes made by Simmons back in the day. I always wondered why my Dad had a 4X Leupold scope on his .22 while I had a Simmons 4X. Although the Simmons did an acceptable job, it was in no way comparable to the Leupold. Of course my Dad's .22 rimfire rifle was also far superior to the Sears model that he bought for me. But believe me, I was just thrilled at age 10 to be able to go squirrel hunting. And since I trained all winter at the local armory, I could hold my own against him.

But enough of the old days. Simmons then was considered a fairly mediocre manufacturer. Now Simmons is a brand owned by Bushnell Corporation (acquired by them in 2008) which in turn is owned by Vista Outdoor. Competition in the optics market and great strides made in this technology has resulted in current offerings superior in quality and also very reasonably priced. That is an example of "value engineering" at its finest.

This Simmons spotting scope was shipped in a hard case and had the scope itself also wrapped in plastic and inside a separate soft case. Well protected indeed! A bench sized tripod is also included as are directions for both locating the instruction manual and for registering the product for potential warranty coverage. Fear not for the instruction sheet is offered in five languages.

Being an older guy and not a hunter, I don't have to worry about lugging this rather large scope through the bushes. However it does serve two needs for me. The first is that it is extremely useful when testing .22 ammo at a 100 yard range. These old eyes are not what they used to be and this Simmons scope makes it simple to track and score my shots. Most of my shooting is suppressed and testing various subsonic ammo has been interesting to say the least.

Since we live on beautiful Charlotte Harbor in Southwest Florida, Mother Nature offers us constant reminders of how the animal kingdom functions and survives. Being able to focus on long distances off our back lanai has really increased our visual reach even to the far shore. We are able to watch Bald Eagles and Osprey fish, Red Tailed Hawks and Florida Barred Owls home in on their prey, and alligators and manatees cruise through the harbor. Entertaining for us and our guests.

For roughly $150.00 this is a heck of a deal for the quality you receive. Simmons has worked its way back into being competitive with most of the mainstream firms. If you're looking for a big increase in quality, plan on spending a lot more money. In the old days we would call this "the law of diminishing returns". That means that you have to spend a lot more money just to get an incremental return in actual performance. Simmons proves that you don't have to spend that much.
text_fidelity_b: Simmons 20-60X60 Venture Black Fmcwptripodhard/Soft Case

text_fidelity_a:
sixthreezero EVRYjourney Women's Electric Bike, 7-Speed Step-Through Touring Hybrid eBike, 26 Inch Wheels This review is for the sixthreezero EVRYjourney Women's Step-Through 500-Watt Electric Bike

The short version is: This is a great bike, sixthreezero has great support, and I highly recommend the bike and company.

My mom has some back issues, including fused vertebrae, and over the years, the number of physical activities she's able to participate in has declined. Long family bike rides on a normal bike were no longer an option. For that reason, in February we decided to go to a local Pedego store and rent e-bikes for my mom and wife. We did a 15 mile ride, and everyone, including my mom and wife, loved it.

My mom liked it so much that she reconfirmed the prices when we got back, but it was definitely outside of her budget.

We both spent the next several months looking for an e-bike deal that was too good to say no to. There's some cheap options online, a Costco mountain e-bike, some nice bikes that are out of our budget, both online and locally, but nothing that was amazing...

Until Prime Day 2019.

sixthreezero's 250-watt bikes were on sale during Prime Day. I don't even see them available now, but it was a great deal, and I did some research before phoning my mom and telling her I think we'd found the deal she was looking for. After telling my mom about it, she ordered one, then asked if I was getting one for my wife. I was on the fence, because it's still a lot of money, until she said, "Don't think about how much you're spending per ride. Do you want to have lots of happy memories of the family riding together or are you OK without those?"

Well said, Mom. I ordered one the next day.

Now, I don't see the 250-watt bikes on Amazon anymore, but when they were here, the online documentation, both here and over at sixthreezero at the time we ordered made the basic functionality seem the same between the 250-watt and the 500-watt bicycles. The key feature both my mom and wife were looking for was the ability to pedal with adjustable resistance, but leverage the throttle with the left thumb to accelerate with the motor when needed to either catch up quickly or tackle hills without issue. (And without changing the level of pedal assistance.)

Some of our first impressions were not great. My mom's bike showed up looking amazing, and my dad assembled it without issue, but the throttle did not behave as expected. (The boost was limited to the level of pedal assist you were in.) My wife's bike showed up, but the fender and rack were both badly bent.

Before buying the bike, I saw that sixthreezero, if you bought directly from them, was willing to offer 365 day test drives, and seemed really focused on customer satisfaction. The Amazon reviews seemed positive, and the box the bike came in offered free assembly at a local bike store. (I'm not sure how that works because I've built over a dozen bikes and this bike is easy to assemble.) That said, I had a damaged bike and it didn't perform as I was expecting. I was definitely concerned when I reached out to sixthreezero.

After multiple calls, photos and a video to confirm that my 250-watt bike did not perform the way their 500-watt did (the technician I was working with only had a 500-watt readily available to troubleshoot with), they were willing to work with my mom and I to find a satisfactory proposal that would allow us to send back the 250-watt bikes and they would ship us 500-watt versions.

They were polite and reasonable throughout the process, but I was still nervous about bike number two, since the first bike did arrive with issues outside of the e-bike functionality. I was pleasantly surprised that they seem to have people working there who seem to genuinely want to make sure their customers love their bikes.

The 500-watt bike went together very easily, and after assembling and tuning the bike, I took it for a ride. The bike was a blast.

The only thing that jumped out at me as being substantially different from the Pedego my wife rode was the seat post. The Pedego had a shock in the seat post, which doesn't do a lot, but is better than nothing. I ordered a "Sunlite Pillar Suspension Seat Post, 27.2 x 350mm, Silver" from Amazon, which seemed like a good improvement to the bike, which is otherwise fantastic. (The rigid seat post makes the ride a tad rough, which is why I gave comfort 4 stars, I'd bump that to 5 with the suspension seat post.)

My wife says she finds the sixthreezero 500-watt basically the same as the Pedego. I'm sure there are differences, but the only big one we see is the price.

I can't adequately describe an e-bike in words alone, but if you have the option to rent one locally, I highly suggest you try it. It's a lot of fun. I'm not a fan of skilled cyclists tearing up mountain bike trails with heavier, faster e-bikes, nor would I advocate road bikers throw electric motors on their bikes, but the joy e-bikes are able to bring families by leveling the field for families that want to ride together is awesome. And sixthreezero's EVRYjourney cruiser is a fantastic bike for those people.

We're averaging speeds of more than half a mile per hour more as a family than we used to, and my wife comes home with a smile on her face while my kids come home having used up more energy and me having gotten a better work out. I know this bike is not cheap, but I like the way my mom put it to me:

Would you rather be out riding with your loved ones? This is a fantastic option for those who can't match the speed or stamina of the people they're riding with.
text_fidelity_b: sixthreezero EVRYjourney Women's Electric Bike, 7-Speed Step-Through Touring Hybrid eBike, 26 Inch Wheels

A Mustard Seed Toys Tungsten Putty Weight, 1 oz, Get The Perfect Weights for Your Pinewood Car to Win Your Derby I've been working on pinewood derby cars for a while. I first started with my children, then the past 10 years holding derby car clinics.

Tungsten putty is important to get your car to maximum weight. I keep the unassembled car weighted at 4.9 ounces. I drill a shallow 1/4 hole under the car and pack in the tungsten putty to make up the last bit of weight. That way on race day you can make small weight adjustments without trashing your car. The fastest car is the heaviest.

I've been getting tungsten putty from the large online derby suppliers. I figured I'd save money in shipping, use Amazon prime, and try a new product. This putty is less dense than the putty I've worked with in the past. It seems to have more sticky binder and less tungsten powder than what I've used in the past. I ordered 3 units. They easily fit inside one container. I even mixed some tungsten powder to the 3 blobs of putty.

I prefer the stuff I got before but this will work

text_fidelity_a:
Sunny SF-B1110 Indoor Cycling Bike I used to be a very active and fit person. I spent 12 years in the Army and as recently as 10 years ago was still running 3 miles a day. However the past 10 years have not been kind; I've gotten older (51), I work at a desk all day and have gotten fat (50lbs+ overweight) and have started having problems with my feet and knees. I knew I needed to get back in shape, but running was out due to my feet and knees. Seeing the Peloton advertisements on TV got me interested in spinning as it seemed like an intense workout that wouldn't kill my feet and knees. Looking into Peloton and seeing the insane price for the bike and classes, and the fact that to use their classes you need an iPhone, iPad, or Apple TV I started looking around for something more affordable that would work with something besides Apple.

That research led me to the Sunny SF-B1110. Based on other reviews the bike had everything that I was looking for; heavy flywheel, sturdy construction, handlebars adjustable front and back and up and down, not noisy and the price was right ($279.99).

I ordered the bike and it arrived in three days. The box it arrived in had slight damage to the outside which is not unexpected with the weight of the item, but the bike itself was packed and cushioned quite well and had no damage. The bike comes 90% assembled, so the only things you need to put together are the front and rear stabilizer bars (the bars that sit on the floor, four bolts total), mount the handlebars and post, mount the seat and post, attach the pedals and you're done.

PROS:
- Price
- Solid Construction
- Fit and Finish
- Quiet Chain Drive
- Smooth Resistance Adjustment
- Front and Back Handlebar Adjustment
- Flywheel Weight

CONS:
- Seat
- Only Three Up/Down Handlebar adjustment holes

Once assembled the bike itself really good looking. The paint is thick and clean, chrome is well done, flywheel is well balanced and spins with no wobble. Chain is quiet and smooth and the resistance adjustment knob works smoothly (doubles as the emergency brake).

The seat that the bike comes with is one of the cons. It's hard, cheaply made and painful to use, especially if you are overweight. Some people will claim you just need to get used to the narrow seats that seem to be the norm now, but the kind of pain this seat caused you can't get used to. I purchased this seat for the bike, [[ASIN:B000H87PUI Sunlite Cloud-9 Bicycle Suspension Cruiser Saddle, Cruiser Gel, Tri-color Black]] and it made all the difference in the world. I highly recommend it and it attaches to the seat post with no modification.

The other con is the vertical adjustment of the handlebars. The handlebar post has only three adjustment holes (the seat post has five). I'm a little over 6 feet tall and have the seat adjusted to its highest point point which puts the seat higher than the handle bars at their highest adjustment point. This very uncomfortable, especially if you have a big belly like I do. I solved this issue by drilling two additional adjustment holes in the handlebar post. There was plenty of room for the additional holes, so why the manufacturer didn't do this is not clear. The handle bars now sit slightly higher than the seat and is much more comfortable.

I also purchased several other items to go with the bike. For anybody that's out of shape you really need to use a heart monitor to make sure you aren't harming yourself by overdoing your workout. I ordered the [[ASIN:B00INQVYZ8 Wahoo TICKR Heart Rate Monitor for iPhone & Android]] and it works very well with my android phone. I also ordered the [[ASIN:B00L9XNFPY Wahoo RPM Cadence Sensor for iPhone, Android and Bike Computers]] to help me sync my workout with the class I'm taking. I also added these clipless pedals [[ASIN:B0014UG3WE Shimano PD-A530 Sport Dual-sided Pedal]].

As far as the classes, I found SweatStudio online classes. Unlike Peloton, they work with Android, PC, Roku, Chromecast, etc. and they have more than spin (yoga, TRX, etc.). I cast my classes onto my 51 inch TV which is much better than some 9 inch tablet.

So for about $500 and some customizing I've got a full workout setup. So far I've lost a few pounds, but more importantly my heart and lungs are getting noticeably stronger. I can't recommend this bike more highly.
text_fidelity_b: Sunny SF-B1110 Indoor Cycling Bike

Positives: it works, its durable, the casing does not get super hot so you won't burn your self if you have to move it,  and it packs down small. Areas for improvement: First, I think the air flow holes/vents need to be a bit larger. After burning some wood some of the ash began to clog up the holes which did not allow good air flow. Second, (probably my biggest concern) it is difficult to keep adding fuel to this stove. Once you put the pot on top of it...it only leaves a small gap so in order to keep adding fuel you have to remove the pot for a second to add fuel so when you take the pot off the direct heat it starts to cool down. It would be nice if it had a cut out on one of the sides to be able to add wood without removing the pot. It took about 20 minutes to get a nice boil for two cups of water. So if you have time to just kick back not a big worry but if you are on the trail and want to stop for a quick lunch probably not the stove for you. Overall, I am glad I have it but probably will use it for emergencies and not so much on the trail.

text_fidelity_a:
POWERBREATHER Wave Snorkel I am rating two stars because it does NOT perform as promised in an important area AND because the company never responded to my request for support.

First, I'm an experienced swimmer; I'm 60+ but I can still swim a mile in under 30 mins and complete a 200 IM, so it's not like I don't know what I'm doing in the water. I've tried and tried -- and really tried -- to love this.

Pluses: SWIMMING with the Powerbreather is a breeze, and I actually enjoy the stress it places on my lungs, forcing me to breathe deeply. When I am swimming point to point I can work on my stroke, don't have to gasp to breathe, etc.

Negative: But doing flip turns is a nightmare! No matter what configuration I try, when I flip the tube fills w/ water and, because it is LITERALLY screwed onto the head, I have to race to release it before I am breathing water. Choking, gasping... this is not my idea of a good time. I've re-read all the literature, and everything points to my being able to do flip turns, which is specifically why I purchase the most expensive version, the Wave. I've reviewed all their pictures and videos, and notice that NOWHERE do they demonstrate anyone doing a flip turn using the device. Interesting. I've written to their customer service on their website asking for help and complaining I can't complete a flip turn w/o taking on water and is there any help they can offer and... crickets. Nothing.

I even had a swimming buddy try out the unit, thinking that "maybe it's me... maybe my flip turns are off." Nope, he took on water, as well.

text_fidelity_a:
Lite Holster Stretch, Expandable, Secure Flashlight Holder with Belt Clip, Universal Sizing, Black My use is for 1" diameter by 5" long tactical lights which do not protrude out the bottom. I also tried it with a 2 C cell light which protrudes out the bottom a lot.

I was looking for something either with a flap cover or a snug but easy to insert fit. This is neither. It has no cover flap, but has a VERY snug fit on this type of light. However it is made up of a series of internal flaps and elastic straps you have to guide the light through to get it into this case. You cannot easily do this one handed as you have to spread two internal flaps apart and hold them that way to insert the light. In addition if you have to sit/stand as in driving patrol or the like, the light works it's way out the top even if it doesn't protrude out the bottom. Since there is nothing to lock it in, the movement of sitting and moving around when seated pushes against the bottom squeezing the light upward like squeezing a toothpaste tube. Eventually it pops out the top. In addition if your light has a tailcap switch it will get turned on without your knowing it in daytime (you would see the light at night), draining the batteries, as there is nothing protecting the tailcap switch from being pressed against the seat bottom.

From my experience with it, this is pretty useless if you are going to be wearing it on a belt in the vertical position, whether a short small diameter or longer larger diameter light. As a temporary worklight holder it isn't bad, but how often do you need a worklight on your belt?
text_fidelity_b: Lite Holster Stretch, Expandable, Secure Flashlight Holder with Belt Clip, Universal Sizing, Black

Not the MOST comfortable thing I've sat on, but it's not a couch, so it's fine. The tension goes up to 14. With being pretty out of shape I can use it on 10 and it's not too hard. The panel is simple, keeping track of time, distance, calories burned and split rate. The app can be a little glitchy, but overall not bad once you get the hang of it. I've not used the upgraded package on it, keeping with the basic that's free and it's fine. I'm not looking for trainer led workouts, and if I was I can find them on youtube. Overall it was a great purchase, and a great deal! I'm very happy with it!

text_fidelity_a:
ALEX Toys Little Jumpers Trampoline 786 I do not recommend the Alex Little Jumper Trampoline unless space is an issue. For $23 less you can purchase the significantly larger and more stable [[ASIN:B008BIV87M Bazoongi 48" Trampoline Bouncer with Easy Hold Handle Bar - Sunshine Yellow. Special Exclusive Limited Edition]].

The instructions are worthless. For example, one part states to "attach the bungee cord to the cord lock by pulling the knotted end of the cord tight". Can I just start by saying "What?" Well there is no knotted end, so you have to create it, though it doesn't really tell you how to do that. Then you have the issue of only three helpful images for the entire manual. And I probably need to start by saying I like to consider myself rather capable when it comes to assembling items and frames of structures having helped my father build our homes and additions. The instructions also do not elaborate where the knotted end should go in reference to the trampoline itself. You can figure out where it needs to go in the medal cord lock, but not on the trampoline itself. The only picture shows half of the trampoline having the cord wrapped around it so you are left wondering what the starting point looks like.

I hazarded a guess and just went with it at that point. Once I wrapped everything around and made sure that I pulled the cord tight several times I then tied it off. The instructions are then once again really vague; therefore I knotted the last end of the cord by itself and pulled it through the medal fastener. I then proceeded to knot the last end of the cord that I had just wrapped around with the beginning part of the cord to ensure an additional sense of security. The instructions mention nothing of this but after looking at the final results, with pieces of cord jutting out in random places, I knew that my three youngest would see that as an invitation to mess with it. So I knotted both ends together, and I did that twice. My kids can be rather problematic.

The directions then tell you to place the cover on the trampoline, making sure that it fits. Once again, the instructions lack on details. They do not specify that the cover should be placed in a specific direction. I used the writing on the cover as an indication for direction, placing the writing outwards where the handle will go. Otherwise, the cover does not fit. I found this out through trial and error, of course. There are also plastic clips that apparently must be clipped to the trampoline in some fashion, that you obviously have to figure out on your own. The most obvious thing was to clip them to the bungee cords that were wrapped around the trampoline.

The next step is to secure the handle. And yet again, those wonderful directions prove that they are pointless. I finally just put the small yellow bar into the curved handle portion (not attaching to the trampoline base yet) to get a sense of where it should go in the actual trampoline frame. I was then able to figure out which direction it faced, knowing that screws would be added at the end. REALLY not clear, but I was able to figure out having put together dozens of pieces before.

All in all, given that it was purchased at a discounted price, it will work out fine in addition to our other in home trampoline. This might be alright for one child, but it would definitely not work for my three kids (4 yr old twins and a 2 yr old) if I did not have the second larger trampoline. They are the ultimate test in terms of durability for any toy and this one is unfortunately not built for heavy duty usage. This might be fine on its own for occasional use from a calmer child, which none of mine are.
text_fidelity_b: ALEX Toys Little Jumpers Trampoline 786

text_fidelity_a:
Alloy Car Roof Bike Bicycle Fork Mount Carrier Rack Max Load 44 lbs After reading the pros and cons of fork-mounting vs upright (wheel-mount) I decided to go with these, figuring the mostly aluminum structure would last a while and the fork-mounting would secure the bikes well. I've used the product one time on a short trip, but so far it seems sturdy and the bikes are locked on firmly. My one concern, which I knew in advance of purchase, is that the fork mount only holds the traditional thin skewers/axles. That works fine for our family fleet of tourers and hybrids from years 1998 through about 2012. However, a lot of new bikes now have the much fatter through-axles (particularly bikes w/ disc brakes). So if i get a new bike I'll probably need a new rack.

Vehicle: 2016 Subaru Outback

Pros:
-My big Cannondale Adventure 400 and my wife's Giant Sedona fit perfectly and are secured with front quick release and included rear hold-down strap.
-Reasonable price, though not as inexpensive as some all-steel models out there.
-No tools required, no customization needed for our Outback with factory folding roof rack.
-Seems and looks solid for those worried about appearance.

Cons:
-May need to fiddle with how many spacers to use with each bolt. There are six bolts on each rack.
-Installation, certainly the first time, might take up to 20 minutes for each rack. And sometimes it's hard to get those big wingnuts to thread properly given the awkward angle since the bolt is vertical and you may not have much space to install the wingnut between bolt and roof of car.
-Very easy to have the spacers fall off the bolts before wingnut is threaded. I had two or three roll off the back of our vehicle. No biggie on a flat concrete driveway but can be a problem on gravel or camping.
-It doesn't lock, which is okay for our needs. I can probably run a cable lock through the frame/tires and part of our roof rack. This may not keep the racks from being stolen but it would be a real pain to remove with bikes mounted. -Of course, it's nice to leave the rack on all summer if you use it frequently, but note someone can get a rack off in 3 minutes if there's no bike on it.
-For any roof rack, it may take a little strength and height to put the bike on top of a car/SUV and simultaneously align that front fork with the locking axle (built into the rack). I'm over 6 feet but my wife is 5'-6" - no way can she use this rack w/ her hybrid. Might be different w/ an ultra-light tourer and a foot stool.
text_fidelity_b: Alloy Car Roof Bike Bicycle Fork Mount Carrier Rack Max Load 44 lbs
